fields.complete_source:
Solution:
Suppose that (V, T1) and (V, T2) are two trees defined over a common vertex set
V . Prove that for every edge e in the edge set T1, there exists a corresponding edge f in T2
such that exchanging these edges preserves the tree structure for both graphs; that is, prove
that (V, (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f}) and (V, (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e}) are both trees.
Suppose that (V, T1) and (V, T2) are two trees defined over a common vertex set V .
Prove that for every edge e ∈T1, there exists a corresponding edge f ∈T2 such that
(V, (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f}) and (V, (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e}) are both trees.
Let G1 = (V, T1) and G2 = (V, T2) be two trees on the finite vertex set V with |V | = n.
Let e = {u, v} be an arbitrary edge in the edge set T1.
Since T1 is a tree, the removal of the edge e disconnects T1 into exactly two connected
components. Let Cu be the component containing u and Cv be the component containing v.
Let Vu = V (Cu) and Vv = V (Cv) be the vertex sets of these components. The sets Vu and
Vv form a partition of V , defining a cut (Vu, Vv).
A set of edges T ′ forms a tree on V if and only if T ′ is connected and |T ′| = n −1. Since
|T1 \ {e}| = n −2, adding any edge f creates a set of size n −1. For the resulting graph to
be a tree, it must be connected. The graph (V, (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f}) is connected if and only if
the edge f connects a vertex in Vu to a vertex in Vv.
Consider the tree T2. Since T2 is connected, there exists a unique simple path P connect-
ing vertices u and v. Let this path be denoted by the sequence of vertices and edges:
u = w0, e1, w1, e2, . . . , ek, wk = v
where ei = {wi−1, wi} ∈T2 for 1 ≤i ≤k.
Since u ∈Vu and v ∈Vv, the path starts in the set Vu and ends in the set Vv. Therefore,
there must exist at least one edge in the path P that crosses the cut (Vu, Vv). That is, there
exists an index j such that wj−1 ∈Vu and wj ∈Vv (or vice versa). Let f = ej = {wj−1, wj}.
We claim that this edge f ∈T2 satisfies the required conditions.
Claim 1:
(V, (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f}) is a tree.
Proof. As established in Section 1, T1 \ {e} consists of two disconnected components on
vertex sets Vu and Vv. The edge f = {wj−1, wj} has one endpoint in Vu and the other in Vv.
Thus, adding f reconnects these two components. The resulting graph is connected and has
n −1 edges, so it is a tree.
Claim 2:
(V, (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e}) is a tree.
Proof. Consider the graph T2 ∪{e}. This graph contains n edges and n vertices. Since T2
is a tree, adding the edge e = {u, v} creates exactly one cycle, which consists of the edge e
combined with the unique path P between u and v in T2. The edge f lies on the path P, so
f is part of this unique cycle. Removing any single edge from a cycle in a connected graph
leaves the graph connected. Thus, removing f from T2 ∪{e} breaks the cycle but preserves
connectivity. The resulting graph is connected and has n −1 edges, so it is a tree.
We have shown that for any edge e ∈T1, there exists an edge f ∈T2 (specifically, an
edge on the path between the endpoints of e in T2 that crosses the cut defined by T1 \ {e})
such that exchanging these edges preserves the tree structure for both graphs.
1
fields.explanation: Keep T1=T2=K2 and their sole edge e. Set insertion leaves one edge, which differs from n=2; both inputs are trees and e lies in each. The headline proves Mathlib IsTree, actual edgeFinset membership, unchanged insertion, and cardinality not two. It suffices to refute the quoted conjunction by its edge-count assertion. The former custom cycle-rank arithmetic and tree surrogate are unnecessary.
fields.flaw: For the arbitrary edge e in T1, the proof claims that T2 ∪ {e} has n edges and that adding e to the tree T2 creates exactly one cycle.

Problem Statement
Problem: Algorithms - 36
Suppose that (V, T1) and (V, T2) are two trees defined over a common vertex set V . Prove
that for every edge e in the edge set T1, there exists a corresponding edge f in T2 such
that exchanging these edges preserves the tree structure for both graphs; that is, prove
that (V, (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f}) and (V, (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e}) are both trees.
1

fields.witness: Take V={1,2}, T1=T2={{1,2}}, and e={1,2}. Both input graphs are trees and e lies in T1. Since e already lies in T2, T2 union {e}=T2 has one edge, not n=2 edges, and remains acyclic. This refutes the local cycle-creation step. The final exchange theorem is not refuted: choosing f=e preserves both trees.
